narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. At 20, it sits far below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, signaling that the model saw this as a major risk for bar exam success.

Next, your first-year law school grades pulled the prediction in the opposite direction. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) still contributed some positive signal toward passing, though its effect was smaller than the LSAT’s negative impact. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10, slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, added a modest additional nudge toward failure.

Your family income, part-time enrollment plan, and third-year grades played only minor roles and were not decisive.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your LSAT score through intensive preparation, as this was the dominant reason for rejection. Strengthening your early law school performance and considering full-time study could also help. Retaking the exam with a significantly higher score and reapplying would be the clearest next step.
